blocks.text: "Big Salad," a fundraising gala held each year for the party's most important political figure.
Iowa Gov. Tom Vilsack was in attendance.
In his speech, he praised the crowd, saying it's made up of "people who have a big stake in the future of Iowa." Indeed it does.
But the "Big Salad" is just about the only way these donors get a chance to meet in person.
There are plenty of other avenues for political fundraising, especially online.
And there are lots of other opportunities for political discussion as well.
But how many chances do most Iowans have to meet directly with a political figure whose decisions will affect their families in the coming years?
There aren't a lot. Sure, there may be some who travel the state, but few Iowans have any real connections to them.
Even fewer meet them. And without personal connections, it's easy to discount them.
So how can we get reacquainted with our state leaders?
How can we make their opinions seem more relevant to our lives?
How can we make our communities and our state more democratic?
In a word: conversation. If you really want to meet the candidate in a way that will make you a real "stakeholder" in Iowa's future, you've got to talk to him.
A big hall and a big salad can be nice, but when a conversation starts, it's the best way to make sure your needs are heard and your concerns are addressed.
But as you try to build a relationship with someone in power, you've got to ask yourself: What can I offer this person besides money?
I think the question is much bigger than that.
For one thing, you're an Iowa voter.
You're a fellow Iowan. Why should a state leader take time out of his day to meet you?
Because you have a right to meet and ask questions of your state leaders.
That's how democracies work.

blocks.text: DNA to investigate criminal cases, family history and identity theft.
Abrams, 59, a mother of two daughters, was never a traditional crime lab technician.
With a degree in molecular genetics, she learned about forensic science through her husband.
"I always wanted to combine science with art, but forensics was really science at its best," said Abrams, who lives in North Attleboro, Mass.
With a background in medical research and computer science, Abrams was hired by the Boston police in 2002 to help the homicide unit develop a computer system to store DNA evidence.
In 2003, she joined a small DNA lab as a full-time technician.
In 2008, she was named director of forensic analysis.
She headed the lab's efforts to identify human remains and DNA evidence from the Boston Marathon bombing in 2013.
Last summer, she stepped down to become a private contractor for a DNA lab in Lexington, Mass.
DNA analysis is now commonplace in crime labs nationwide.
It's used in about 25 percent of the 14,000 homicides that happen in the United States every year, according to a 2015 report by the FBI's Uniform Crime Report.
It's commonly used in rape and robbery cases.
DNA analysis is so precise, says Abrams, that a 12-year-old case was solved in 2013.
Police in New York had been trying for 13 years to crack an assault and robbery case.
The suspect was arrested when DNA from the suspect's DNA sample was compared with the DNA found on a woman who had been beaten and robbed in 2000.
The woman reported the crime, but she didn't give a description of her attacker.
Still, the lab matched the woman's DNA to that found at the crime scene.
Then, the DNA lab compared her DNA with a database of convicted felons.

What could have gone wrong,' Weir wrote with one tweet.
'Climate doesn't cooperate with Al Gore's group visit to Denver EPA hearings.
Why not call it rain?,' he later tweeted.

On Thursday, Weir got in a little more trouble for his response - which got hundreds of thousands of views and re-tweets, including one from former President George Bush, who suggested we shouldn't get so worked up over the headline.
But then Weir turned the tables on Bush and said, 'Sorry Mr. Bush, you're not welcome here.' Watch his second tweet here.

"We only really had a small wardrobe and a few of my clothes and our camera gear," Danica says.

"We had nothing in the way of an emergency kit." When the coronavirus hit and restrictions on the movement of people started, Danica soon found she was running low on food and that basic hygiene items were becoming increasingly hard to come by.
"Everything was getting hard to find," she says.
"I wasn't sure we were going to be able to buy enough stuff." So she looked to the community for help, and found it through a local Facebook group.
The group had a section for residents looking for essential items to survive the coronavirus pandemic.
Danica and others would share their needs and what they could do with the items they were getting.
That day, she was able to pick up milk, flour, and frozen vegetables.
In the two months since, the group, now numbering 250 members, has helped the Weeks family get many other items.
They've received boxes and boxes of toilet paper, tissues, cleaning products, vitamins, dog food, and more.
The Facebook group is a small piece of the larger community effort to help each other in a time of need.
"When the pandemic first hit, it was panic buying everywhere," says Paul, who is still in Mongolia.
"I couldn't believe that this many people were stocking up on toilet paper.
I was like, 'It's a pandemic, not the end of the world." Now that the restrictions have started to ease and people are allowed to move around again, the couple says things are getting easier.

blocks.text: this month at the trial of the man accused of killing him.
Michael's father Joe Jackson, an army captain, had served two tours of duty in the Korean War.
He and his wife met as teenagers on the South Side of Chicago and moved to Gary when Michael was 9 months old to get a better job and a bigger home.

The city's black citizens were fleeing northward in great numbers, lured by the auto industry's need for unskilled workers, but the Jacksons found the working-class neighborhood of Washington Park a quiet refuge from the chaos of Chicago.
"Everybody was poor, and everybody was happy," Joe Jackson said in 1991.
"We didn't have a whole lot of money, but we didn't worry about anything.
It was an idyllic situation." There were 12 Jackson children — seven girls and five boys, though only two of the boys grew up to sing.
In the spring of 1959, when the baby was 12 months old, the family moved again, to a spacious brownstone in a nearby, more affluent area called Hinsdale.
Michael's childhood in the neighborhood, according to Katherine Jackson, was idyllic.
"We played ball in the driveway, played football, baseball, stickball," she said.
"Everybody looked out for everybody else.
It was a nice place." The Jacksons lived just a few blocks from the Gary Industrial Museum, now a national landmark, in which workers and their families would gather to enjoy the band on weekends.
